objectives: Outline major imaging modalities + their physics.
Apply CNN/transformer architectures to medical images.
Reason about labels + transfer learning + FDA pathway.

slides.title: Imaging modalities + the physics
slides.body:
**Modalities** + characteristic uses:

**X-ray** (radiograph):
- Photons through tissue; differential absorption by density.
- Bone bright (high absorption), air dark.
- Cheap, fast, low radiation (~0.1 mSv).
- Uses: fractures, pneumonia, dental.
- 2D projection; overlapping anatomy.

**CT (Computed Tomography)**:
- X-ray with rotational source-detector; reconstruct 3D from projections.
- ~5-15 mSv per scan.
- Resolution: ~0.5-1 mm.
- Uses: trauma, stroke (non-contrast head), cancer staging, pulmonary embolism (CTPA), coronary artery disease.
- Slices reconstructed in axial, coronal, sagittal.

**MRI (Magnetic Resonance Imaging)**:
- Strong magnetic field (1.5-7T) aligns hydrogen nuclei; RF pulse excites; relaxation signals detected.
- No ionizing radiation.
- Excellent soft-tissue contrast.
- Slower than CT (~30-60 min).
- Multiple sequences: T1, T2, FLAIR, DWI, contrast-enhanced.
- Uses: neuro, MSK, cardiac, abdominal, breast.

**Ultrasound**:
- High-frequency sound waves; reflected at tissue interfaces.
- Real-time, portable, no radiation, cheap.
- Operator-dependent.
- Uses: obstetrics, cardiac (echocardiography), abdominal, vascular, point-of-care (POCUS).

**Nuclear medicine (PET, SPECT)**:
- Radioactive tracer; gamma cameras detect emissions.
- Functional imaging (metabolic, perfusion, receptor binding).
- Fused with CT or MRI for anatomical context (PET-CT, PET-MRI).
- Uses: oncology (FDG-PET), cardiology (perfusion), neuro (amyloid, dopamine).

**Pathology**:
- **H&E (hematoxylin + eosin)**: standard histology stain.
- **IHC (immunohistochemistry)**: antibody-targeted staining.
- **Digital pathology**: whole-slide imaging (WSI) at ~0.25 μm/pixel; gigapixel files (>1 GB per slide).
- Increasingly: AI-augmented diagnosis.

**Ophthalmology**:
- **Fundus photography**: retinal images.
- **OCT (Optical Coherence Tomography)**: cross-section retinal layers.
- Diabetic retinopathy + glaucoma + macular degeneration screening.

**Dermatology**:
- **Dermoscopy**: handheld microscope with polarized light.
- Smartphone images: increasingly used for AI screening.

**Cardiology**:
- ECG (1D waveform, deep history of ML).
- Echocardiogram (ultrasound).
- Coronary CT angiography.

**File formats**:
- **DICOM**: medical imaging standard. Embeds image + patient + acquisition metadata.
- **NIfTI**: neuroscience research.
- **NDPI, SVS**: WSI for pathology.
- Data volumes: huge. CT ~500 MB, MRI brain ~200 MB, WSI ~1-10 GB per slide.

slides.title: CNNs + transformers for medical imaging
slides.body:
**Why CNNs work for medical imaging**:
- Translation invariance (lesion can be anywhere).
- Hierarchical features (textures → patterns → objects).
- Parameter efficiency vs fully-connected.

**Common architectures**:
- **U-Net** (Ronneberger 2015): encoder-decoder with skip connections. Workhorse for SEGMENTATION. Endless variants (Attention U-Net, nnU-Net, TransUNet).
- **ResNet**, **DenseNet**, **EfficientNet**: classification backbones.
- **Mask R-CNN**: instance segmentation.
- **3D CNNs**: for volumetric (CT, MRI). Expensive.
- **Vision Transformers (ViT)**: increasingly used.
- **Swin Transformer**: hierarchical, efficient.
- **SAM (Segment Anything Model, Meta 2023)**: foundation model for segmentation. MedSAM, SAM-Med2D adaptations.
- **Foundation models**: BiomedCLIP, MedSigLIP, ChEX, RAD-DINO. Pretrained on millions of medical image-text pairs.

**Tasks**:
- **Classification**: image-level label (e.g., normal vs pneumonia chest X-ray).
- **Detection**: bounding box around finding (e.g., nodule detection on CT).
- **Segmentation**: pixel/voxel-level masks (e.g., tumor boundary on MRI).
- **Registration**: align images (e.g., longitudinal MRI for change detection).
- **Generation/synthesis**: denoising, super-resolution, modality translation (CT → MRI), missing-data imputation.
- **Report generation**: image → text findings (CheXagent, RaDialog).

**Transfer learning**:
- ImageNet pretraining works surprisingly well even for medical (Raghu et al 2019).
- Medical-specific pretraining (RadImageNet, MedCLIP) increasingly competitive.
- Self-supervised pretraining: SimCLR, MoCo, MAE → label-efficient.

**Self-supervised + contrastive**: when labels expensive. Pre-train on huge unlabeled image set, fine-tune on small labeled set. Common in pathology + radiology.

**Annotation challenges**:
- **Expert time**: only specialists can label (radiologists, pathologists). Expensive (~\$200/hr).
- **Inter-annotator variability**: even experts disagree. Multi-annotator consensus.
- **Pixel-level labels**: very time-consuming. ~1 hour for a CT scan segmentation.
- **Weakly-supervised**: image-level labels (from reports), bounding boxes; multiple-instance learning.
- **Active learning**: model selects uncertain cases for labeling.
- **Pseudo-labels**: use a strong model to label, then train another model.

**Pre-processing**:
- Intensity normalization (CT HU windowing, MRI N4 bias correction).
- Skull stripping (brain MRI).
- Resampling to common voxel spacing.
- Cropping/padding to fixed input size.
- Augmentation: rotation, flip, elastic deformation (preserves anatomy), intensity jitter, MixUp.

slides.title: Deployment + regulation + the SaMD pathway
slides.body:
**Software as a Medical Device (SaMD)**: regulated by FDA + EU (MDR) + others.

**FDA pathways** for AI/ML medical devices:
- **510(k) clearance**: substantially equivalent to predicate device. Most common (~90%).
- **De Novo classification**: novel device, low-moderate risk.
- **PMA (Premarket Approval)**: high-risk; rigorous trial data.
- **Breakthrough Designation**: priority review for unmet need.

**FDA AI/ML approvals**:
- ~1000+ approved AI/ML medical devices (FDA list updated 2024).
- Most: radiology (~75%), cardiology, ophthalmology, pathology.
- Examples: IDx-DR (diabetic retinopathy, 2018 first autonomous), Caption Guidance (echo), Aidoc (radiology triage), Viz.ai (stroke triage), Paige Prostate (pathology).

**Locked vs adaptive algorithms**:
- **Locked**: fixed model post-clearance. Standard.
- **Adaptive (predetermined change control plan, PCCP)**: model can be retrained per protocol. New 2023+ FDA framework.

**Performance requirements**:
- Demonstrate clinical performance on representative population.
- Stratified analysis (age, sex, race, ethnicity, imaging device, site).
- Compare to standard of care.
- Post-market surveillance.

**Regulatory considerations beyond FDA**:
- **CE Mark (EU)**: MDR (Medical Device Regulation) — stricter than old MDD.
- **MHRA (UK)**: post-Brexit; mostly aligned with EU.
- **PMDA (Japan), NMPA (China), TGA (Australia), Health Canada**.

**Bias + equity**:
- Training data often biased toward majority populations.
- Performance gaps across race, age, geography common.
- Sources: data imbalance, label bias, label definition, deployment context.
- Mitigations: diverse training data, fairness-aware training, stratified evaluation, ongoing monitoring.
- High-profile examples: dermatology models with poor performance on dark skin, sepsis prediction models with race disparities (Obermeyer 2019).

**Real-world deployment challenges**:
- **Distribution shift**: test population differs from training. Hospitals, scanners, populations.
- **Workflow integration**: model must fit clinician workflow. Worklist priorities, EHR integration, time per case.
- **Adoption**: clinicians + administrators need to trust + use the tool.
- **Liability**: who's responsible for AI errors? Open legal questions.
- **Reimbursement**: CMS gradually adding codes for AI services.
- **Monitoring**: drift detection, performance tracking.

**Major use cases by modality**:
- **Radiology**: triage (Viz.ai stroke), nodule detection (CT lung), measurement (cardiac function), report generation, prioritization.
- **Pathology**: prostate Gleason grading, breast IHC quantification, search/retrieval.
- **Cardiology**: ECG (Apple Watch AFib, Eko stethoscope murmurs).
- **Ophthalmology**: diabetic retinopathy, glaucoma, macular degeneration.
- **Dermatology**: lesion classification.
- **Surgery**: AI-assisted endoscopy, surgical guidance.

**Foundation models in radiology** (2023+):
- BiomedCLIP, MedCLIP, BiomedGPT.
- CheXagent, RaDialog, MAIRA.
- Goal: chatbot-style image interpretation.

question.question: Why U-Net for segmentation
question.goal: U-Net (Ronneberger 2015) is THE workhorse architecture for medical image segmentation. Why does it work so well?

steps.prompt: U-Net has an encoder (downsampling) + decoder (upsampling) with SKIP CONNECTIONS between corresponding levels. Why are skip connections critical?

options: Skip connections preserve SPATIAL DETAIL: encoder loses resolution (downsampling) but gains semantic context. Skip connections feed high-resolution low-level features into decoder upsampling → output retains pixel-precise boundaries needed for segmentation.

steps.reveal: Skip connections preserve high-res features. Without them, output is semantically aware but blurry. Segmentation needs pixel-precise boundaries; skip connections bridge encoder semantics + decoder spatial detail.

steps.prompt: U-Net was originally designed for biomedical (cell + neuron) segmentation. What made medical-image segmentation specifically suited to U-Net?

options: Medical images: limited data (so parameter-efficient architecture matters); precise boundaries critical (clinical decisions hinge on exact tumor edge, vessel lumen); structured anatomy (skip connections leverage anatomical consistency). U-Net's small parameter count + boundary-preserving design fit perfectly.

steps.reveal: Medical segmentation: small labeled sets (expert annotation expensive), need precise boundaries, structured anatomy. U-Net's parameter efficiency + boundary preservation fit. Larger models without these properties (early ViTs) underperformed until adaptations.

steps.prompt: Modern: nnU-Net (Isensee 2021) automates U-Net configuration for any medical-image segmentation task. Why has this 'just configure U-Net well' approach often beat fancier architectures?

options: Most medical segmentation benchmarks: nnU-Net wins. Key insight: careful preprocessing + appropriate input size + training schedule + ensembling matters more than architecture novelty. nnU-Net auto-configures these. Lesson: in narrow domains with limited data, mature simple architectures + tuning > fancy new models.

steps.reveal: nnU-Net showed: careful engineering (preprocessing, input size, training schedule, ensemble) > novel architectures for medical segmentation. Wins ~80% of medical-segmentation challenges. Lesson applies broadly: in data-limited domains, mature architectures + thorough engineering often outperform new arch ideas.

question.finalResult: $$\boxed{\text{U-Net: encoder-decoder + skip connections; nnU-Net auto-configures + ensembles}}$$ U-Net's enduring relevance + nnU-Net's dominance demonstrate that ARCHITECTURE plus ENGINEERING > architecture alone in data-limited domains. Modern medical-segmentation foundation models (MedSAM, SAM-Med2D) are improving but nnU-Net remains a strong baseline. The bitter lesson cuts both ways: scale wins eventually, but for many specific clinical tasks careful tuning still leads.

question.question: An FDA-approved chest X-ray model performs 5 percentage points worse on darker-skinned patients in deployment. Likely cause + fix?
options: Training data underrepresented darker-skinned populations OR label biases (whose chest X-rays get labeled how). Fixes: enrich training data, fairness-aware training, stratified evaluation + monitoring. FDA increasingly asks about demographic performance + post-market surveillance.
question.explanation:
Common bias source in medical AI: training data reflects historical care patterns (who got imaged, who got labeled, by whom). Darker-skinned patients underrepresented in many training sets. Labels may be biased (different documentation patterns). Result: model accuracy varies across demographics.

Famous examples: dermatology models trained mostly on lighter skin perform poorly on darker; pulse oximeters less accurate on darker skin (hardware issue, but parallel); Obermeyer et al 2019 found a sepsis prediction tool underestimated risk for Black patients because it used healthcare costs as a proxy.

Mitigations: (1) Enrich training data with diverse populations. (2) Stratified evaluation across demographics. (3) Fairness-aware training. (4) Post-deployment monitoring + drift detection. FDA increasingly mandates demographic subgroup analysis + post-market surveillance. The shift to 'algorithmic fairness in healthcare' is active research + policy area.

slides.workedSolution: Training data + labels reflect historical care patterns; underrepresented populations get worse predictions. Fixes: diverse training data, fairness-aware training, stratified eval, monitoring. FDA increasingly mandates demographic analysis. Famous: dermatology models on darker skin; Obermeyer 2019 sepsis model. The field is actively responding.

FDA pathway for an AI radiology tool
question.prompt: Your startup developed a chest X-ray AI for triaging pneumonia. Walk through the FDA 510(k) pathway.
Explain in two or three sentences why medical-imaging AI is the most-approved category of FDA AI/ML medical devices.
question.rubric: Mentions that medical imaging has well-defined input (image), clear clinical task (detection/classification/segmentation), abundant existing ML methods (CNNs), and clear deployment workflow (PACS integration). Other modalities (clinical notes, decision support) face workflow + interpretability + liability challenges that make regulatory + commercial path harder. ~75% of FDA AI/ML approvals are radiology + cardiology imaging.
